blocks.text: A man whose seizures have been controlled on carbamazepine for years has a chest infection and is given an antibiotic that is later found to inhibit the same enzyme pathway that clears his anticonvulsant. Three days later he is ataxic, diplopic and vomiting with a toxic drug level. Nothing was wrong with either prescription on its own. Interactions are the dangers that appear only when two safe prescriptions meet.

blocks.markdown: A **drug interaction** occurs when one drug (or food, herbal product or alcohol) alters the effect of another. **Pharmacokinetic** interactions change how much drug reaches the site of action by altering absorption, distribution, metabolism or excretion. **Pharmacodynamic** interactions change the response at a given concentration, by additive, synergistic or antagonistic effects, and they may involve drugs with unrelated kinetics. Whether an interaction matters clinically depends on the size of the effect, the drug's **therapeutic index**, patient factors (renal and hepatic function, age, number of medicines) and whether the effect can be monitored or managed.

rows: Absorption
Chelation or binding in the gut lumen
Calcium, iron or antacids reducing absorption of tetracyclines or ciprofloxacin
Metabolism: induction
Increased enzyme synthesis (often CYP3A4) so clearance rises and drug levels fall
Carbamazepine or rifampicin lowering the effect of the combined oral contraceptive pill
Metabolism: inhibition
Competitive or irreversible enzyme blockade, clearance falls and levels rise
Clarithromycin raising exposure to drugs cleared by CYP3A4
Excretion
Reduced renal clearance or tubular secretion
NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors or thiazide diuretics raising lithium levels
Transport (P-glycoprotein)
Reduced efflux or renal secretion of substrate
Amiodarone or verapamil raising digoxin levels
blocks.caption: Principal pharmacokinetic interaction mechanisms. Check the BNF interactions appendix for severity and advice.

blocks.markdown: For a drug given by repeated dosing and cleared by first-order processes, the average steady-state concentration depends on the dosing rate and the clearance. If an interacting drug halves clearance, the steady-state concentration doubles at the same dose; if clearance rises, concentrations fall. The time to approach steady state depends on the half-life, with about 97% reached after five half-lives, so effects of an interaction may take days to appear and days to resolve.

blocks.caption: R_0 is the dosing rate (mass per time) and CL is clearance (volume per time), assuming constant bioavailability and linear kinetics.
Half-life depends on the volume of distribution V_d and clearance CL; time to near steady state is about 5 t_{1/2}.

blocks.title: Estimating the effect of enzyme inhibition
blocks.prompt: A hypothetical drug X is cleared mainly by CYP3A4, and its clearance is 10 L/hour. A new CYP3A4 inhibitor lowers its clearance to 6.25 L/hour. The dose is unchanged. By what factor does the average steady-state concentration change, and what should the prescriber do? (Values are for teaching only.)

steps.text: Write the relationship: at constant dosing rate, concentration is inversely proportional to clearance, so C_new / C_old = CL_old / CL_new.
Substitute: 10 / 6.25 = 1.6. The average steady-state concentration rises by a factor of 1.6, which is a 60% increase.

Judge the clinical importance. For a drug with a wide therapeutic index this may be tolerable; for a narrow-therapeutic-index drug or one with concentration-dependent toxicity (for example a statin causing myopathy) a 60% rise may be unacceptable. The change appears over about five half-lives of X.

Act: check the BNF interaction entry and the product information. Options are to avoid the combination, choose a non-interacting alternative, withhold the substrate drug for the short course, or reduce the dose and monitor. Inform the patient of symptoms to report.

blocks.answer: Concentration rises by a factor of 1.6. Whether to avoid, withhold or monitor depends on the therapeutic index and the BNF advice.

rows: Enzyme inducers
Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort
Lower levels and reduced effect of substrates; effect develops over days to weeks and persists for some time after stopping
Enzyme inhibitors
Clarithromycin, erythromycin, azole antifungals, ritonavir, grapefruit juice
Higher levels and increased toxicity of substrates; onset usually within days
Other examples
Amiodarone (multiple pathways), ciprofloxacin (CYP1A2)
Raises levels of substrates such as warfarin or theophylline; check the BNF
blocks.caption: Common inducers and inhibitors. Not every member of a class interacts equally; consult the BNF.

rows: Additive sedation or respiratory depression
Opioids with benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids or alcohol
Profound sedation and respiratory depression
Additive QT prolongation
Citalopram with erythromycin or ondansetron; low potassium or magnesium makes it worse
Torsades de pointes risk
Serotonin toxicity
SSRI with tramadol, linezolid or an MAO inhibitor
Agitation, tremor, hyperthermia, clonus
Additive hyperkalaemia
ACE inhibitor or ARB with spironolactone, potassium supplements or trimethoprim
Dangerous hyperkalaemia
Additive bleeding
Warfarin or DOAC with NSAIDs, aspirin or SSRIs
Haemorrhage
Opposing effects
Sildenafil with nitrates (profound vasodilatation)
Severe hypotension; this combination is contraindicated

blocks.title: Narrow therapeutic index
blocks.text: A narrow therapeutic index means the concentration or dose that gives benefit is close to the concentration that causes toxicity, so small changes in exposure (from an interaction, impaired clearance or dosing error) can cause treatment failure or serious harm. Narrow-therapeutic-index medicines usually need monitoring of levels or effect.

blocks.markdown: Examples of narrow-therapeutic-index medicines include **warfarin**, **digoxin**, **lithium**, **phenytoin**, **theophylline**, the **aminoglycosides** such as gentamicin, **ciclosporin** and **tacrolimus**, and **methotrexate** (with its serious toxicity if mis-dosed). Other **high-risk medicines** carry harm because of how they are used rather than their index alone: **insulin**, **anticoagulants** and **opioids** are repeatedly implicated in serious medication incidents.

headers: Key monitoring (check BNF, local protocol and service guidance)
rows: Warfarin
Bleeding or clotting from INR out of range; many interactions
INR, with frequency set by the anticoagulation service and increased when interacting drugs start or stop; target range depends on indication
DOACs
Bleeding; accumulation in renal impairment
No routine coagulation test; renal function, full blood count and liver function periodically, with dose adjusted to renal function
Insulin
Hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemia, dosing in the wrong units
Capillary glucose, HbA1c; prescribe doses in 'units'; do not omit basal insulin in type 1 diabetes
Opioids
Sedation, respiratory depression, constipation, accumulation in renal impairment
Sedation, respiratory rate, pain score, bowel function; review dose in renal impairment
Aminoglycosides, vancomycin
Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity
Drug levels per local protocol, creatinine or eGFR, avoid other nephrotoxins
Lithium
Toxicity with dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides
Serum level at the specified time after the dose, renal and thyroid function
Methotrexate
Bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity; fatal errors if taken daily instead of weekly
Full blood count, liver and renal function, with intervals set in shared-care protocols
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs
Acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia
Urea and electrolytes and creatinine before and after starting or changing dose
blocks.caption: Monitoring requirements are summarised; always follow current BNF, local and specialist guidance.

blocks.title: Building a monitoring plan for an inpatient on several high-risk medicines
blocks.prompt: A 72-year-old man admitted with an infected foot ulcer is on warfarin for atrial fibrillation, basal-bolus insulin, regular intravenous gentamicin and oxycodone as required for pain. His eGFR is mildly reduced. Outline a monitoring plan.

steps.text: Warfarin: new antibiotics and acute illness change the INR, so check the INR more frequently than usual according to the anticoagulation service, review the next dose daily against the result and watch for bleeding.

Insulin: capillary glucose monitoring around meals and at bedtime per local protocol, adjusting doses for reduced intake, infection and steroid exposure; prescribe in units written in full; do not omit basal insulin without advice.

Gentamicin: baseline and daily creatinine or eGFR, drug levels timed according to the local protocol, avoid other nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs, and ask about hearing, tinnitus and balance. Reduced eGFR means accumulation risk, so follow the local dosing protocol and pharmacy advice.

Oxycodone: assess pain, sedation and respiratory rate after doses, check bowel function, avoid other sedatives, and recognise that reduced renal function increases accumulation. Check doses and renal advice in the BNF.

blocks.answer: Increase INR and glucose checks, monitor renal function and gentamicin levels daily per protocol, and assess sedation and respiratory rate for opioids, with doses checked against the BNF.

blocks.title: Interaction checking is not a substitute for thinking
blocks.text: Interaction software and the BNF flag severity, but alert fatigue is real. Always ask: what is the mechanism, which patient is at risk, how will I detect harm, and is there a safer alternative? Stopping an inducer can cause toxicity of a drug whose dose was previously raised to compensate.

points: Interactions are pharmacokinetic (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion) or pharmacodynamic (additive, synergistic or antagonistic effects).
Inducers lower and inhibitors raise levels of substrates; at constant dose, steady-state concentration is inversely proportional to clearance.
Narrow-therapeutic-index drugs (warfarin, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, aminoglycosides, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, methotrexate) need monitoring and extra caution.
Anticoagulants, insulin, opioids and nephrotoxic drugs need specific monitoring such as INR, glucose, sedation and respiratory rate, and renal function and drug levels.
Use the BNF and local protocols for severity, doses and monitoring intervals; the principles here guide where to look.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an enzyme-inducing drug?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin and St John's wort are classic inducers that lower the effect of substrates. Macrolides, azoles and some quinolones are inhibitors.

options.text: Clarithromycin
Rifampicin
Fluconazole
Ciprofloxacin

distractorRationale.b: Correct: rifampicin induces cytochrome P450 enzymes and reduces levels of many drugs.
distractorRationale.d: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, so it raises levels of substrates such as theophylline.

questions.stem: A woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill is started on carbamazepine for epilepsy. What is the principal reason her contraceptive protection may fail?
questions.explanation: Enzyme induction takes days to weeks to develop and persists after the inducer is stopped. Prescribers must advise on alternative or additional contraception according to current guidance.

options.text: Carbamazepine delays gastric emptying and reduces absorption of the pill
Carbamazepine induces hepatic enzymes, accelerating the metabolism of the pill's hormones
Carbamazepine displaces the hormones from plasma proteins
Carbamazepine inhibits renal tubular secretion of the hormones

questions.correctOptionText: Carbamazepine induces hepatic enzymes, accelerating the metabolism of the pill's hormones

distractorRationale.a: Absorption is not the main problem.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: enzyme induction increases hormone clearance and lowers concentrations; check current UK contraception guidance and BNF.
distractorRationale.c: Protein-binding displacement is rarely clinically important and does not explain this.
distractorRationale.d: That mechanism would raise, not lower, hormone levels.

questions.stem: A patient stable on lithium starts regular ibuprofen for back pain. What is the most likely consequence?
questions.explanation: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and renal elimination. NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and thiazide diuretics all reduce its clearance, so levels should be checked and the combination avoided where possible.

options.text: Reduced lithium absorption and loss of mood control
Reduced renal lithium clearance, raising lithium levels with a risk of toxicity
Increased lithium metabolism by the liver
No effect, because lithium is not renally excreted

questions.correctOptionText: Reduced renal lithium clearance, raising lithium levels with a risk of toxicity

distractorRationale.a: Absorption is not significantly affected by NSAIDs.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: NSAIDs reduce renal lithium excretion, so levels can rise towards toxicity and need checking.
distractorRationale.c: Lithium is not metabolised by the liver.
distractorRationale.d: Lithium is excreted almost entirely by the kidneys, which is why renal function matters.

questions.stem: Which of the following medicines has a narrow therapeutic index?
questions.explanation: Digoxin, warfarin, lithium, phenytoin and aminoglycosides are classic narrow-therapeutic-index medicines. Their levels or effects need monitoring and interactions matter.

options.text: Amoxicillin
Digoxin
Cetirizine
Omeprazole

distractorRationale.a: Amoxicillin has a wide margin between effective and toxic doses.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: digoxin has a narrow margin, and toxicity occurs at levels close to therapeutic ones.

questions.stem: Which statement about monitoring a patient taking a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: DOAC dosing depends on renal function, so reduced clearance raises bleeding risk. The frequency of checks should follow the BNF and the product information, with closer review in older or renally impaired patients.

options.text: The INR should be checked weekly to adjust the dose
No routine coagulation test is needed, but renal function and blood count should be checked periodically because the dose depends on renal function
Monitoring is unnecessary once the first prescription is issued
A daily blood level is required

questions.correctOptionText: No routine coagulation test is needed, but renal function and blood count should be checked periodically because the dose depends on renal function

distractorRationale.a: The INR is used for warfarin, not for routine DOAC monitoring.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: DOACs are not monitored with a routine coagulation test, but renal function and blood count checks are needed; follow the BNF and product information.
distractorRationale.c: Periodic review is needed because renal function changes and bleeding can occur.
distractorRationale.d: DOAC levels are not routinely measured.

questions.stem: True or false: enzyme induction usually develops gradually over days to weeks and can persist for a time after the inducer is stopped.
questions.explanation: Induction requires increased synthesis of enzyme protein, so it develops and recedes slowly. Stopping an inducer can therefore lead to rising concentrations of a substrate drug whose dose had been increased to compensate.

options.text: True
False

questions.stem: A CYP3A4 inhibitor lowers the clearance of a drug from 12 L/hour to 4.8 L/hour. The dose is unchanged. By what factor does the average steady-state concentration rise?
questions.explanation: At a constant dosing rate, steady-state concentration is inversely proportional to clearance. The ratio is 12 divided by 4.8, which equals 2.5, so the concentration rises 2.5-fold, which could be dangerous for a narrow-therapeutic-index drug.

questions.stem: A narrow-therapeutic-index drug has an elimination half-life of 18 hours. After an interaction or dose change, approximately how long will it take to reach about 97% of the new steady state, taking this as five half-lives? Give the answer in hours.
questions.explanation: About 97% of steady state is reached after five half-lives, so 5 multiplied by 18 hours is 90 hours. This is why levels checked too early after a change can mislead and why interaction effects may take days to appear.

questions.stem: Describe why methotrexate is regarded as a high-risk medicine and set out the monitoring and prescribing precautions that apply, including an example of an important interacting drug.
questions.explanation: A strong answer ties toxicity to narrow index, highlights the weekly-dosing error trap and names an interaction with a mechanism. Monitoring intervals come from the specialist protocol and the BNF.
markingGuide: Narrow therapeutic index, with dose-related and idiosyncratic toxicity including bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity and mucositis
Weekly dosing for most non-oncology indications, with serious and sometimes fatal errors if taken daily; prescribe and counsel the day of the week explicitly
Monitoring: full blood count, liver function and renal function, with intervals set by the shared-care protocol, the BNF and the specialist
Renal impairment reduces clearance and raises toxicity risk
Interactions: trimethoprim or co-trimoxazole (additive antifolate effect, avoid), NSAIDs reducing excretion; check the BNF
Counsel the patient on warning symptoms such as sore throat, bruising and mouth ulcers, and document clearly

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has been stable on warfarin for atrial fibrillation. He is started on rifampicin as part of treatment for a bone infection. Explain what is expected to happen to his anticoagulation, why, and how you would manage and monitor it, including what happens when rifampicin is later stopped.
questions.explanation: The key point is that both starting and stopping an inducer change warfarin requirements, in opposite directions. Frequent INR monitoring bridges the changes safely.
markingGuide: Rifampicin is an enzyme inducer that increases warfarin metabolism, so INR falls and anticoagulation becomes inadequate with stroke risk
Induction develops over days to weeks, so the effect appears gradually
Management: warn the anticoagulation service, check the INR frequently and adjust the dose to the target range as advised by the BNF and local service
When rifampicin is stopped induction wanes over weeks, so the INR rises and the dose must be reduced, with a risk of bleeding if not anticipated
Monitoring should be intensified at both the start and the end of the course, and the patient should be told about bleeding symptoms
Consider whether a different anticoagulant or a different antimicrobial is suitable, with specialist advice
